missed.claim: M2 — There is no epoched public entry that accepts a pre-positioned `ParserState`, so the unsound raw entry is not consumer misuse: it is the ONLY mechanism for a legitimate use case the tree itself exercises.
missed.proof: `Parser.parseState(val: string)` (parser.ts:34) and `Parser.parse(val)` (parser.ts:77-78) both construct a fresh state at offset 0 (`new ParserState(val)`, parser.ts:52) and there is no overload, no `parseFrom(src, offset)`, and no `parseState(state)`. `packratEnter`/`packratExit` — the only scoping handles — are published by neither entry (index.ts:8, packrat-entry.ts:5). This is precisely what parse-that's own >1MB soundness test does (reentrancy.test.ts:204-211). C-1 grades the invariant "unenforced and undocumented" (challenge-C-consumption.md:145-148) and C-12 notes the missing scoping primitive (:387-396), but neither states the sharper consumption fact: the documented surface is INCAPABLE of the use case, so "a disciplined consumer never trips this" (C-1's reachability note at :143-145) is unavailable to any consumer with a non-zero start offset. superlatives: S-1 CONFIRMED — the float64-safe memo key with a fail-loud boundary is exemplary. packrat.ts:52-77 derives the budget (32-bit offset span, ≈2²¹ id headroom, 32+21=53) rather than hard-coding it (`MEMO_MAX_ID = Math.floor(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER / MEMO_OFFSET_SPAN)`, :77), :79-89 documents the exact defect it cures WITH its aliasing witness (`getCijKey(4096,0) === getCijKey(0,0)`), and :90-98 throws rather than aliases at the ceiling. Both former hazards are pinned executably: memoize.test.ts:161-175 (the int32 `<< 20` overflow) and reentrancy.test.ts:185-194 + :196-213 (the >1MiB cross-offset case). Choosing fail-loud over silently-wrong at a numeric boundary, and writing the derivation into the source, is the standard the rest of this audit should be held to. (C-8 disputes WHERE the throw surfaces, not the choice.)

S-2 CONFIRMED — the epoch save/restore is the right shape, in the right place, with the right unwind, and the interface is provably set-equal to the state it protects. `interface PackratEpoch` (packrat.ts:196-202) lists memo/heads/growing/lrStack/currentSrc; the module declares exactly those five globals (:133-135, :186, :193); packratEnter snapshots all five and installs empties (:218-230) and packratExit restores all five (:243-250). The call site wraps `parseStateInner` in `try/finally` (parser.ts:43-48) and `growLR` mirrors the discipline internally (:390-406). Nested top-level parses are re-entrancy sound AND the parent is uncorrupted on a throw, at one object per parse — which is exactly why C-3's crash arm stays contained to the throwing parse.

S-3 CONFIRMED — arming at construction rather than first invocation is the subtle, correct ordering, and it is a theorem rather than a race. `PACKRAT_ARMED = true` is the FIRST statement of makeMemoized (packrat.ts:290), before `p` is even bound at :292, and the reasoning at :146-155 is right: arming at first invocation would leave that invocation's own `packratEnter` (parser.ts:43) already returned unarmed, so the first memoized parse would run epoch-less. You cannot obtain a memoized parser without having armed. The one hole is the lazy back-edge (`Parser.lazy(() => memoize(...))`, lazy.ts:20-22), filed as C-15 and confirmed at MINOR — retention, not a wrong answer. It does not diminish the design.

S-4 CONFIRMED — `proof:packrat-armed` is a gate that proves its own non-vacuity. It subclasses the global `Map` BEFORE importing the built dist so it counts real allocations (scripts/proof-packrat-armed.mjs:58-66), warms one parse outside the window (:100), asserts an exact count of 0 over N=5,000 non-memoized parses (:138-146), and then spawns a CHILD process that deliberately constructs a `memoize()` and asserts allocation DOES occur (:110-133 under `PACKRAT_POISON`, launched at :151-154) — closing both false-green paths (dead counter, broken latch). It also records WHY it refuses a throughput-% threshold (:29-32, a confirmed flake trap). L-19 met in-tree; and, read the other way, it is the project's own written admission of C-2.

S-5 (MINE) — the `./packrat` TYPE routing is minimal and honest, and it is what keeps my M1 at MINOR. package.json:24 points the subpath's `types` at `./dist/packrat-entry.d.ts`, whose entire content is one line re-exporting exactly `memoize, mergeMemos, resetPackrat` — NOT at the 5-export `dist/packrat.d.ts`. So the surface a consumer can NAME equals the surface they can CALL, and `getCijKey`/`packratEnter`/`packratExit`/`PackratEpoch` are invisible through the published subpath. Leaking internals through a barrel is the default outcome of a dts plugin; routing types at the entry declaration instead is a deliberate, correct choice.

S-6 (MINE) — the zero-consumer state is provable by MANIFEST and packed artifact, not merely by grep, so the retirement decision needs no consumer survey. The dependency's removal is a nameable event (`164343c1`, whose diff carries `-"@mkbabb/parse-that": "^1.0.0"`); today `grep -c parse-that package.json` → 0, `node_modules/@mkbabb/` holds only glass-ui/keyframes.js/value.js, the packed `@mkbabb/value.js@4.0.0` declares `dependencies: undefined`, and the two surviving "parse-that" strings in `src/` are assertions of the absence (src/subpaths/math.ts:2, src/subpaths/transform.ts:4). An absence that is asserted in the source it is absent from is a much stronger record than a sweep that found nothing.

S-7 (MINE) — the X·P §4 "WRAP the RangeError into a value" verdict is not aspirational: the landing type is already published and frozen downstream. value.js's 52-export `/css` surface exports `ParseIssue` and `ParseResult` (src/css/index.ts:20-21), defined at src/css/types.ts:10 as a `Readonly<{...}>` and at :25-27 as a discriminated union whose failure arm is `{ ok: false; diagnostics: readonly [ParseIssue, ...ParseIssue[]] }`. missed.claim: The caret is drawn at the pre-truncation column against a line `summarizeLine` has already re-windowed, so every failure display for a source line longer than 74 characters points at the wrong place — usually past the end of the rendered line.

In `summarizeLine` (:14-31) with `len > MAX_LINE_WIDTH` (74, :10) and `start > 0` (:22), the return is `"..." + trimmed.slice(start, end) [+ "..."]`, so the accused character now sits at index `3 + (columnNum - start)`. Trace, ASCII only: line length 200, columnNum 100 → half=37, start=63, end=137, rendered line = 3+74+3 = 80 chars, target index = 3+37 = 40; the caret is drawn at column 100 — 60 cells right of the target and 20 cells past the end of the line. Second trace (the `end >= len` branch): length 100, columnNum 90 → start=53, rendered = 3+47 = 50 chars, target index 40, caret at 90. The prefix width is not the confound: with colour enabled the escapes are zero-width so the gutter is `lnWidth + 4` cells either way, which is why the `start === 0` branch (:25-26) IS correctly aligned — the defect is exclusively the un-shifted column. This is the common case for minified CSS, JSON, and any single-line document — precisely the corpus the X·P band parses. challenge-L-library.md:212-225 (D6) inspected `debug.ts:83` and `:116` and attributed misalignment solely to display width (CJK, tab, emoji), missing the ASCII truncation window entirely; challenge-C-consumption.md does not examine the caret at all.

superlatives: S1 — CONFIRMED, and C's framing is the sharper of the two. The conjunction order in src/parse/ansi.ts:4-6 makes the un-chained `process.env` dereference unreachable in shim environments: it is evaluated only after `process.stderr?.isTTY === true` has proven a Node-shaped process. Under the standard bundler shim (`globalThis.process = { env: {} }` from vite-plugin-node-polyfills / webpack ProvidePlugin) `typeof process !== "undefined"` is true and `process.stderr` is undefined, so the `?.` is the one character between correct evaluation to `false` and a top-level `TypeError` at module evaluation. Verified to hold in the ARTIFACT, not just the source: dist/packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js:28 and dist/packrat-entry-46NYx4_U.cjs:29 carry the expression verbatim — and because that chunk is imported by dist/core.js:1, dist/parse.js:1, dist/utils.js:2 and dist/packrat.js:1, the un-chained form would have taken down four of five published subpaths at import time in every browser bundle. `=== true` rather than truthiness is the second half of the same discipline. challenge-L-library.md:250-261 (S1) and challenge-C-consumption.md:197-199 (S-3).

S2 — CONFIRMED. `!process.env.NO_COLOR` (src/parse/ansi.ts:6) is exactly the current no-color.org rule on the two edges implementations miss: `NO_COLOR=""` leaves colour ON (spec: present AND non-empty), `NO_COLOR="0"` turns it OFF (presence, not truthiness). Both rows are arithmetic on `!` and need no run. A `Boolean()`-parse gets the first wrong; a `=== "1"` test gets the second wrong; `"NO_COLOR" in process.env` over-triggers on the bare `NO_COLOR=` common in .env files. The one-character check is right by construction. Scope limit found in this re-read: this is the opt-out half of the convention only — the TTY half ignores TERM entirely (missed M-3). challenge-L-library.md:263-270 (S2), challenge-C-consumption.md:186-195 (S-2).

S3 — CONFIRMED at the ship. When `enabled === false` every one of the ten functions is `return s`: no template literal, no concatenation, no intermediate rope, no String wrapper — the caller's own string comes back by reference. Verified in the built artifact, dist/packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js:29-37, as ten `enabled ? \`…\` : s` ternaries. The industry-standard shape is the opposite (build-then-strip, or a chalk-style proxy allocating a builder per property access), and there is nothing in ansi.ts:8-17 to find on the disabled arm. And the disabled arm is the arm that actually runs: under vitest the process's stderr is piped, so `isTTY` is undefined and every one of the suite's render assertions exercises exactly this path. challenge-L-library.md:272-280 (S3).

S4 — CONFIRMED as a shape claim, with its V8 mechanism killed (see killed K8). Ten flat top-level `const` arrows of the single signature `(s: string) => string`; no factory, no closure-per-call, no class, no property bag, no shared mutable state beyond the one boolean. Every call site is monomorphic by construction and there is no shape to transition — `debug.ts` passes only strings at all 20+ call sites (enumerated for L-D5 above), and `dist/ansi.d.ts` confirms the uniform signature survives to the published types. The claim that V8 will constant-fold the module-context `const` and collapse the disabled arm to the identity function is unmeasured and MEASURE-AT-OPEN; the monomorphism is not, and stands on the source alone. challenge-L-library.md:282-297 (S4).

S5 — CONFIRMED, and independently the strongest craft finding in either document. Each helper terminates with the specific cancel for its own attribute — 22 for intensity, 23 for italic, 39 for foreground, 49 for background — rather than the near-universal shortcut `\x1b[0m`. `grep '\[0m' src/parse/ansi.ts` → no match. This is what makes the four live nesting families render correctly: `bgRed(bold(" Err x "))` (debug.ts:152) and `bgGreen(bold(...))` (:154, :156) keep their background across the inner close, `bold(red(...))` (:78, :239) keeps its bold, `yellow(italic(...))` (:160) keeps its colour. A blanket `0m` closer would have broken all four. L's handling of the residual is also right: SGR 22 being shared between codes 1 and 2 is a property of ECMA-48, unfixable by any choice of closer — the only cure is a nesting-aware attribute stack, which a 17-line module correctly declines to build. challenge-L-library.md:299-308 (S5).

S6 — CONFIRMED with one scope correction. Perfect export/consumer parity at the source tier: all ten exports consumed, by exactly one file, in exactly one import statement (src/parse/debug.ts:5). Verified by the negative grep (`bgGreen|bgRed|italic` outside the ansi/debug pair → zero hits in src and test; the sole filename-sweep hit, test/benchmarks/nearley.ts:116 and :167, is the substring in 'EBNF *-expansion' — confirmed verbatim). killed.claim: CHALLENGE-L:184-186: "`d.line`/`d.column` from `collectDiagnostic` would disagree and expose it — refuted: `utils.ts:107-110` re-implements the same algorithm with the same clamp, so both paths are wrong *identically*. That is why nothing catches it."
killed.refutation: FALSE AT THE BYTES, and it inverts. `utils.ts:107-110` does NOT use the negative-fromIndex clamp: it computes `const before = src.slice(0, furthest)` FIRST, then `before.lastIndexOf("\n")`. At furthest=0, `before` is `""` and `"".lastIndexOf("\n")` is −1 → `line = 1`, `column = 0` — **correct**, where `state.ts:128-132` returns {2, −1}. For every offset ≥ 1 the two are provably identical (the slice bound `lastNl+1 ≤ furthest` makes the split operate on the same substring). So the two implementations disagree at exactly the one offset that matters, in the direction that would have exposed the bug. The doc's stated reason "why nothing catches it" is not the reason; the real reason is that `formatDiagnostic` has no test and no door (its own C·C-14 / M-1). This inverts into a MISSED defect — see missed MISS-1.

killed.claim: CHALLENGE-L:225-233: making the memo write at `debug.ts:340` unconditional "kills the exponential. It also **widens this defect**" — "a one-line fix that trades a performance defect for a correctness defect is worse than the defect."
killed.refutation: NOT ESTABLISHED. Traced at the source: the degraded `"lazy"` placeholder is produced only by the `else` arm at `debug.ts:324-326`, reachable only when `id` is truthy. Dropping the `if (id)` guard adds cache entries **only** for the id-undefined top-level walk, and those entries hold exactly the string the walk already computes — for the L doc's own construction, the delta is `{string("x") → "\"x\"", L1 → "[\"a\", lazy]"}`, both identical to a fresh recomputation. No node acquires a rendering it would not otherwise produce, no read at `:257` changes answer, and the cycle guard at `:320` is untouched (verified for self-recursive and mutually-recursive two-lazy grammars: both still terminate). The unconditional write does kill the exponential (`print(left)` on the second pass hits `:257`). The correction limb is therefore unsupported; the doc's two-part fix (memoize on expansion completion + an explicit `visiting: Set<number>`) is a better design, but not because the one-liner regresses correctness.

killed.claim: CHALLENGE-L:476-478: "It is worse here than at the parse boundary, because this code runs **on the failure path**: the sequence at `parser.ts:67-69` is *parse failed → render → console.error*, so a malformed `src` converts a parse failure into a renderer crash that **buries the original failure**."
killed.refutation: REFUTED on two independent gates. (1) On a non-string `src`, the *parse* throws before any render: every shipped leaf reads `state.src` (`leaf.ts` string/regex scanners, `parser.ts:467` `state.src.length`), so `parseStateInner`'s `this.parser(state)` at `parser.ts:53` throws and `:55-69` is never reached — the very TypeError O-15 PT-07 measures at the parse boundary, not the render boundary. (2) Even for the contrived parser that fails without touching src, the render at `parser.ts:68` is gated on `isDiagnosticsEnabled()` (`:67`), which is `false` by default (`utils.ts:6`). So the renderer-crash-buries-the-failure narrative requires an armed process plus a src-blind failing parser, or a hand-built state passed straight to `statePrint`. The bare fact (no boundary check; raw TypeError) stands and is carried in confirmed at MINOR; MAJOR is a mis-calibration.

killed.claim: CHALLENGE-L:739-740: "A span whose offset exceeds `src.length + lines.length − 1` matches no line."
killed.refutation: ARITHMETIC WRONG, and it understates reach. `debug.ts:107` accumulates `lineEnd = offsetAcc + lines[i].length + 1`, so the terminal accumulator is Σ(lenᵢ + 1) = (src.length − (L−1)) + L = **src.length + 1**. The drop condition is therefore `span.offset > src.length` (i.e. ≥ src.length + 1), independent of L. Worked example, src="ab\ncd" (len 5, L=2): offsets 0–5 match, offset 6 drops; the doc's formula gives 5+2−1 = 6 and says 6 matches. The true threshold is lower and does not grow with line count, so the defect is *more* reachable than filed.

killed.claim: CHALLENGE-L:534-539 and :743: reaching `formatSecondarySpans` "requires `isDiagnosticsEnabled()` (`:174`), and arming is refused under X·P W1 §G-5" — hence both findings are byte-derived only and "marked for execution by whoever holds the arming budget."

The arming budget was never the blocker; the hedge is unnecessary and the two findings could have carried executed evidence.

killed.claim: CHALLENGE-L:239-241 ("`toString` is called implicitly by `${p}`, by `"" + p`, by **`console.log`**") and CHALLENGE-L:503-505 / CHALLENGE-C:157-158 (the same list).

killed.claim: CHALLENGE-C:210-214: "caret column: 158 | overshoot past rendered line: 73" for a 240-char minified line with the error at offset 150.

missed.claim: MISS-1 · MAJOR · A single rendered diagnostic contradicts itself: `formatDiagnostic`'s header prints `line:column` from the `Diagnostic` snapshot, which `collectDiagnostic` computes CORRECTLY at offset 0, while the caret block underneath recomputes position through the buggy `getLineAndColumn`. For a recovered error at byte 0 of a source beginning with a newline, the header says `1:0` and the caret is drawn on line 2.
missed.proof: LIVE: `debug.ts:203` `const locStr = dim(\`${d.line}:${d.column}\`);` takes the position from the snapshot, whose values were computed at `utils.ts:107-110` via `src.slice(0, furthest)` + `lastIndexOf` — correct at furthest 0 ({1,0}). Two lines later `debug.ts:207-208` builds `new ParserState(src, undefined, d.furthestOffset, true)` and calls `addCursor`, which at `debug.ts:59` calls `getLineAndColumn()` → `state.ts:128` `lastIndexOf("\n", offset - 1)` → {2, −1}. So one function emits two mutually contradictory positions for the same byte, in one document, and the correct answer is already in the object it was handed. Neither challenge has this: CHALLENGE-L:184-186 asserts the exact opposite (that both paths carry the same clamp) and uses that false claim as its explanation for why nothing catches B-2. Reach: any `recover()`-collected diagnostic at offset 0 of a newline-leading source — the README's own multi-error workflow (README.md:229-232).

missed.claim: MISS-2 · MAJOR · `formatAllDiagnostics` is O(N × |src|) in both allocation and time: each diagnostic reconstructs a full `ParserState` and re-splits the entire source (twice when secondary spans are present). The function exists for the many-errors case, and it degrades exactly there.
missed.proof: LIVE: `debug.ts:238` `diagnostics.map((d) => formatDiagnostic(d, src))` → per diagnostic, `debug.ts:207` allocates a `ParserState` (5-field object) and `debug.ts:208` → `addCursor` → `debug.ts:58` `state.src.split("\n")` allocates one string per source line, plus `debug.ts:217` → `formatSecondarySpans` → `debug.ts:100` a second full split. Rendering 100 recovered errors on a 100 kB multi-line stylesheet performs 200 full source splits and allocates ~20 MB of line strings to display ~100 carets — for a feature whose entire premise (README.md:216-232, `parser.ts:653-688`) is "keep going and report them all". Nothing in the module hoists the split out of the loop, though `src` is invariant across the whole map. Neither challenge measures the multi-diagnostic path: CHALLENGE-L:439-464 (M-6) scopes its allocation finding to `statePrint` under `parserDebug`, and CHALLENGE-C:485-489 (S-3) files the same `ParserState` reconstruction as a **superlative** ("genuinely economical") on style grounds without costing it. This is the allocation-discipline lens's sharpest miss.

missed.claim: MISS-3 · MAJOR · The `(Diagnostic, src)` API cannot enforce that `src` is the string the offsets came from, and the package's own worked example gets it wrong: it collects diagnostics from `cssWithErrors` and renders them against `css`. Offsets from one source rendered against another produce a caret on a wrong line with no error and no warning.
missed.proof: LIVE: `debug.ts:200` `formatDiagnostic(d: Diagnostic, src: string)` and `debug.ts:235` `formatAllDiagnostics(diagnostics: readonly Diagnostic[], src: string)` take the source as an unpaired second parameter; `Diagnostic` (`utils.ts:84-93`) carries offsets, line, column and a `found` snippet but **no source identity** — no length, no hash, no reference — even though `collectDiagnostic` had `state.src` in hand at `utils.ts:103`. The README's Error-Recovery example is the proof of hazard: `README.md:230` `stylesheet.parse(cssWithErrors);` then `README.md:232` `console.error(formatAllDiagnostics(diagnostics, css));` — two different variables, one line apart, in the package's only worked example of the feature. The renderer silently obliges: `addCursor` clamps its window (`debug.ts:62-63`), so a mismatched source degrades to a confidently-wrong caret rather than a throw. Neither challenge notes it; CHALLENGE-L:245-292 quotes README:232 for the import-path defect and reads straight past the argument mismatch on the same line.

missed.claim: MISS-4 · MINOR · `summarizeLine`'s `trimEnd()` desynchronizes the caret on SHORT lines too — the exact lines both challenges certify as correct. The rendered content is trailing-whitespace-trimmed; the caret pad is not, so the caret overshoots by the trailing-whitespace width. Every CRLF source is mis-pointed by one at end-of-line, and every failure at a `\n` overshoots by the line's trailing padding.
missed.proof: LIVE: `debug.ts:15` `const trimmed = line.trimEnd();` and `debug.ts:19` `if (len <= MAX_LINE_WIDTH) return trimmed;` — the ≤74 fast path still shortens the line; `debug.ts:83` `pad = lnWidth + 4 + columnNum` uses the untrimmed source column. Worked case, src = `"a  \nb"`, error at offset 3 (the newline): `getLineAndColumn(3)` → {1, 3}; `lines[0]` = `"a  "` → `summarizeLine("a  ", 3)` returns `"a"`; rendered line is `" 1 | a"` (content ends at index 5) while the caret sits at index 8 — three columns past a one-character line. Bound is the trailing-whitespace width, which is unbounded (a space-padded column-200 line renders 3 characters and points 197 columns out). CHALLENGE-L:109-142 and CHALLENGE-C:195-229 both scope the coordinate mismatch to `len > 74` ("for lines ≤ 74 chars the pad is correct"), so this second, independent instance is outside both — and it is the one that fires on CRLF fixtures and on the most common failure position of all, end-of-line.

missed.claim: MISS-5 · MINOR · The two renderers disagree about carriage returns: the primary block is CR-safe by accident and the secondary-span block is not. `formatSecondarySpans` emits `lines[i]` raw, so on a CRLF source a bare `\r` lands mid-block and a terminal returns the cursor to column 0 — the following marker line overwrites the source line it annotates.
missed.proof: LIVE: `debug.ts:100` splits on `"\n"` only, leaving a trailing `\r` on every line of a CRLF source; `debug.ts:114` pushes `\` ${gray(...)} ${pipe} ${lines[i]}\` ` — `lines[i]` verbatim, no `trimEnd`, no sanitisation — and `debug.ts:117` then pushes the marker line, which the terminal renders over the top. The primary block escapes only because `summarizeLine` happens to call `trimEnd()` (`debug.ts:15`), which eats the `\r`. Column arithmetic is unaffected and correct (`debug.ts:107` counts the `\r` in `lines[i].length`, matching real source offsets), so this is purely an output-integrity defect. CHALLENGE-L:528-532 notes that `:114` prints raw *and untruncated* but frames it only as a width disagreement with the primary block; neither doc reaches the control-character consequence, and neither considers CRLF input anywhere.

missed.claim: MISS-6 · MINOR · `formatSecondarySpans` throws a raw `RangeError` from `String.prototype.repeat` on a negative span offset — the same untyped-boundary posture as PT-07, on the render path, in a function the module reaches ungated from `formatDiagnostic`.

A negative `span.offset` satisfies `span.offset < lineEnd` on the very first iteration (`debug.ts:108`), so `col` is negative and `lnWidth` is floored at 3 (`debug.ts:110`) → any `span.offset ≤ −8` makes the argument negative and `repeat` throws. `SecondarySpan.offset` is a bare `number` (`state.ts:31-34`) on a public mutable array (`state.ts:45` `secondarySpans: SecondarySpan[] = []`) and on a mutable `Diagnostic` field (`utils.ts:91`), with no non-negativity check at `addSecondarySpan` (`utils.ts:57-61`) or anywhere in the renderer. missed.claim: MISS-7 · MINOR · The grammar printer emits its own metacharacters unescaped, so its output is ambiguous and not round-trippable: `string('"')` prints `"""`, and any terminal containing `|`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `!`, `?`, `<<`, `>>` renders as printer syntax.
missed.proof: LIVE: `debug.ts:269-270` `case "string": return \`"${args![0]}"\`` — raw interpolation, no escaping — against a printer whose grammar vocabulary is exactly those characters (`:281` `!`, `:283` `?`, `:286` `>>`, `:290` `<<`, `:299` `[…, …]`, `:306` `|`, `:312` `{min,max}`). A parser for a CSS delimiter (`string("|")`, `string("}")` — both routine in the band's candidate grammars) prints as a grammar operator, so `all(string("a"), string("|"), string("b"))` renders `["a", "|", "b"]` where a reader cannot tell terminal from alternation. The module is advertised as producing a grammar rendering (README.md:187, api.md:111), and the Rust-isomorphism claim (README.md:207-208) is asserted against shared vectors nothing reads. superlatives: SUP-1 · `formatExpected` (`debug.ts:33-47`) is the module's one total function and the only one pinned by real tests. The 0/1/2 arms return without allocating an intermediate; the n≥3 arm produces a correct Oxford-comma list; the parameter is `readonly string[]` so it cannot disturb what it describes. Four exact-equality assertions cover all four arms (`test/debug.test.ts:53-73`) — the only branch coverage in the file. Falsifier re-tested: duplicate labels would mis-punctuate, refuted upstream at `utils.ts:40` (`if (!state.expected.includes(label))`). Both challenges name it (L·S-1, C·S-1) and both are right; C's added observation — that its signature maps exactly onto value.js's `ParseIssue.expected: readonly string[]` (`src/css/types.ts:22`) — is the sharpest consumption reading in either document.

SUP-2 · `ansi.ts` is 17 lines, zero dependencies, decides once at module scope, and is provably per-symbol tree-shakeable. `ansi.ts:3-6` computes `enabled` from `typeof process !== "undefined" && process.stderr?.isTTY === true && !process.env.NO_COLOR` — the `typeof` guard degrades a browser bundle to plain text instead of throwing, and `NO_COLOR` is honoured without a `supports-color` dependency. NEW EVIDENCE neither doc has: `dim` (`ansi.ts:9`) is the only formatter used exclusively by the shaken-out `formatDiagnostic` (`:203`, `:225`), and it is **absent from the shipped chunk** — `grep -c 'x1B\[2m' dist/packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js` → 0, while the other nine formatters ship at chunk `:29-37`. The palette shakes at symbol granularity, which means the m-13/C-7 pinning cost is precisely the *reachable* renderer and not a byte more.

SUP-3 · `addCursor`'s window arithmetic is total under adversarial input, and that is why B-2 is a wrong answer rather than a crash. `debug.ts:62-63` clamps both bounds (`Math.max(lineIdx - MAX_LINES, 0)`, `Math.min(lineIdx + MAX_LINES + 1, lines.length)`), so no out-of-range index into `lines` is reachable for any `lineNum` — including the out-of-range `line: 2` that the `lastIndexOf` clamp manufactures, and including `lineNum > lines.length`, where `startIdx > endIdx` makes the loop body never run and the function return `""`. Defensive arithmetic that degrades instead of failing, in a renderer that by construction runs on the failure path (`parser.ts:67-69`), is the correct posture. Verified by derivation, not inherited.

SUP-4 · The diagnostic substate is per-parse, not global, and this module is where that choice is honoured. `debug.ts:172-188` reads `state.expected`, `state.secondarySpans`, `state.suggestions` off the *state instance* (`state.ts:43-45`), never a module accumulator — the design `utils.ts:20-26` documents and the reason a nested `.parse()` inside a `.map` callback cannot corrupt the outer parse's error tracking. That is the exact hazard class the packrat tier had to cure with an epoch snapshot and a `try/finally` (`parser.ts:34-49`); the renderer needed no cure because the data was threaded correctly upstream. Falsifier tested: the one global read that could break it (`isDiagnosticsEnabled()`, `debug.ts:174`) affects *whether* extras render, never *whose*, so the reentrancy property genuinely holds — and filing it simultaneously as a superlative and as m-5 is the honest reading.

SUP-5 · The type posture is stricter than the tier below it. Every array parameter in the module is `readonly` — `formatExpected` (`:33`), `formatSecondarySpans` (`:98`), `formatSuggestions` (`:127`), `formatAllDiagnostics` (`:235`) — and all four bodies were read: none writes to its array parameter, so the annotations are not hollow. In 383 lines there is exactly one `any` (`:254`), eslint-disabled with a stated reason. This is sharper than its own dependency: `utils.ts:89-91` declares `Diagnostic`'s three arrays as mutable `string[]`/`Suggestion[]`/`SecondarySpan[]`, which is why `collectDiagnostic` must defensively spread all three (`utils.ts:120-122`) to obtain the immutability this module got from the type system for free.

SUP-6 · The package's own publish-discipline gate is honest about why it exists, and its header is the reason this module's gap is diagnosable. `test/dist-surface.test.ts:6-11` records, in prose, that the shipped 0.8.2 dist exported only 8 of 15 span functions and "the version number lied about it" — a gate authored from a real incident rather than from a checklist, parsing the source barrel's named exports (`:18-34`) and asserting each against `dist/index.d.ts`. It is also the precise shape of the blind spot: it cures source-barrel→dist and leaves published-`.d.ts`→exports-map uncovered, which is exactly the direction `dist/debug.d.ts` fails in. A gate that states its own provenance makes its own boundary auditable — the reason C·C-2 could be filed at all.

killed.claim: 'the primitive tier can consume labelled failures but cannot construct one' (challenge-C:198)
killed.refutation: Over-strong. Four /core leaves seed labels through mergeErrorState with no /diagnostics import: string() at leaf.ts:291/:303 (label `"str"`, built at :278), eof() at leaf.ts:16 (`<end of input>`), dispatch() at leaf.ts:142 (its precomputed `one of [...]` label at :132) and regex() at leaf.ts:360. The precise statement of debt 1's blockage is therefore: /core offers no way to choose the label independently of the pattern, and (per C-5, confirmed) the label is undefined at runtime anyway with diagnostics off. Both halves matter; the second is the binding one and C-4 leaves it to C-5.

missed.claim: M2 - `.trim(p)` SILENTLY DISCARDS `p` whenever `p.context?.name === "whitespace"`, substituting an ASCII-only charCode loop. Consequence: `.trim()` does not implement `.trim(whitespace)`'s own semantics, and two spellings of one documented intent return opposite verdicts on Unicode whitespace. Behaviour is keyed on a mutable public string, not on the parser.
missed.proof: SOURCE parser.ts:480-521: the default parameter is `whitespace` (:481); the branch at :488 tests `parser.context?.name === "whitespace"`; the returned closure `whitespaceTrim` (:498-512) calls trimStateWhitespace(state) and inner.parser(state) and NEVER references `parser` again - the argument is provably dead on that path. trimStateWhitespace (leaf.ts:372-391) accepts only charCode 32 and 9..13; the `whitespace` singleton it stands in for is regex(/\s*/) (leaf.ts:397), whose class additionally includes U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000-200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000 and U+FEFF. API-TEST vs dist/core.js, decisive pair on ONE regex source: const xs = regex(/x*/) named 'regex' -> string('a').trim(xs).parseState('xxaxx').isError = FALSE (argument honoured); the SAME pattern with xs.context = createParserContext('whitespace', undefined) -> string('a').trim(xs).parseState('xxaxx').isError = TRUE (argument discarded, the charCode loop runs instead); and .trim(xs, false), which routes to all(), = FALSE again. Unicode divergence: string('a').trim().parseState(NBSP+'a'+NBSP).isError = TRUE while string('a').trim(regex(/\s*/)).parseState(NBSP+'a'+NBSP).isError = FALSE; whitespace.parseState(NBSP+'x').value = NBSP while trimStateWhitespace leaves offset at 0. TYPE-LEGAL for consumers: 'whitespace' is a member of the exported parserNames union (state.ts:158, :174), so createParserContext('whitespace', ...) is the sanctioned spelling; and whitespace.context.name is a plain mutable string on an exported singleton (API-TEST reads 'whitespace'). WHY IT MATTERS HERE: challenge-C:134-137 and challenge-L:82-87 both observe that the fast path 'routes around' the exported combinator and treat it purely as the thing that MASKS B-1. It is also an independent wrong-answer defect in the opposite direction, it is the reason C-8's consequence clause is backwards (killed K5), and under W2.md's EQ-1 exact-equality law a whitespace class that differs between two spellings of the same operator is a divergence source a lowering pair cannot reconcile.

missed.claim: M4 - No .d.cts anywhere in dist, so the types served under every `require` condition are ESM declarations for CJS implementations - the classic 'masquerading' shape, in a package that is "type": "module".

TypeScript determines a .d.ts file's module format from the nearest package.json `type`, so dist/core.d.ts is read as an ES module while dist/core.cjs is CommonJS. A TS consumer on moduleResolution node16/nodenext emitting CJS resolves the `require` condition and then cannot import the ESM-typed declaration (TS1479); are-the-types-wrong classifies this as FALSE_ESM. Nothing in the five gate scripts checks the types-vs-implementation format pairing: manifest-gate.mjs:43-47 only asserts that exports['.'].types EXISTS, and subpath-gate.mjs:29-35 only stats the file. So a classic-resolution consumer gets 'Cannot find module @mkbabb/parse-that' with no diagnostic pointing at the cause. missed.claim: M7 - dispatch()'s undocumented 3-character range heuristic silently reinterprets literal multi-char keys, and an inverted range maps nothing while the label advertises it.
missed.proof: SOURCE leaf.ts:116 `if (chars.length === 3 && chars[1] === '-')` fires for ANY 3-character key whose middle character is a hyphen - there is no opt-in marker. The JSDoc at leaf.ts:86-87 documents multi-char keys ('tf' = 't' or 'f') and range keys ('0-9') as coexisting spellings, so `dispatch({ 'a-b': p })` is ambiguous by the doc's own rules and is silently taken as the range a..b: tbl[97] and tbl[98] are written at :119 and the hyphen (charCode 45) is never mapped, though the multi-char reading would have mapped it. Inverted ranges are worse: 'z-a' gives lo=122 > hi=97, so the `for (let c = lo; c <= hi; c++)` at :119 executes zero times and the key maps NOTHING, while the label builder at :129 renders it as "'z'-'a'" - a diagnostic advertising a dispatch that does not exist. This is D-13's silent-key class a second time on the same function, and it is live for CSS: the hyphen is an ident-start in custom properties (--x) and vendor prefixes (-webkit-), so a head table over {hyphen, digit, letter} is exactly the shape a 3-character key gets written in.

missed.proof: SOURCE leaf.ts:335-343: `const execResult = sticky.exec(state.src); const match = matchFunction!(execResult);` - the user callback is invoked even when exec returned null, so every matchFunction must handle null and nothing says so. `if (match)` then `else if (match === "")` makes the empty string a THIRD outcome distinct from null - zero-width success via state.ok(undefined) at :342, with sticky.lastIndex never consulted - so a callback that legitimately extracts an empty capture group gets a non-consuming success rather than consuming its match. On the truthy arm, :340 advances by `sticky.lastIndex - savedOffset`, i.e. by the REGEX's match length regardless of what the callback returned, so a normalizing callback that returns a shorter or longer string still consumes exactly the raw match. None of this is in a doc comment - regex() has none - and the parameter is on the /core surface (core.ts:22).

superlatives: S1 (L S-2, verified EXACT and the best thing in the package) - getCijKey is a model of naming a numeric-precision hazard and gating it. packrat.ts:70-100: the PREVIOUS bug is named in full (`parser.id << 32` overflowing int32 at id >= 4096, so getCijKey(4096,0) === getCijKey(0,0)), the replacement is derived from the float64 mantissa ceiling with the 32+21=53-bit budget shown, MEMO_MAX_ID is computed at :77, and the boundary FAILS LOUD with a RangeError at :94-97 rather than aliasing. Every line cite in L's S-2 is byte-exact. Hazard named, bound computed, gate installed, history retained - and D-13's silent Int8Array key write is the same hazard class handled the opposite way two files over, which is what makes D-13 sting.

S2 (L S-5 / C S-3, verified verbatim) - the PT-Q5 RETRACT docblock, leaf.ts:88-98. A shipped 0.12.0 perf widening is DELETED because it had zero production consumers and was gated against a synthetic corpus no consumer runs, with the re-entry condition stated in advance and anchored to a named consumer's real grammar ('If value.js's coordinated Q session measures an on-path win ... not before'). Retracting one's own optimisation for want of a real consumer, in writing, is the rarest discipline in a performance-oriented library.

S3 (L S-1, verified across every combinator) - the zero-allocation result discipline is real and uniformly held. state.ts:55-73 (ok/err/from) mutate in place and return `this`; every one of the ~24 combinators in parser.ts and leaf.ts threads ONE state object with a `savedOffset` local for backtracking, and I found no exception. The consistency is the achievement: one combinator returning a fresh state would poison the invariant.

S4 (L S-3, re-traced) - the re-entrancy hardening is sound at two levels. parser.ts:43-48 wraps parseStateInner in try/finally around packratEnter/packratExit; packrat.ts:390-406 wraps growLR's grow loop in a second try/finally restoring per-head GROWING/HEADS bookkeeping. The PT-Q1 regression this replaced (per-node reset inside memoizeFn, wiping an outer grow's cells) is preserved with its exact failure mode at packrat.ts:159-172. Fixing a re-entrancy bug AND leaving the falsified prior design in the tree as a warning is rare.

S5 (L S-6, verified) - the two classic combinator footguns are both closed, one with its rationale. many() guards zero-width matches at parser.ts:538; sepBy() checkpoints BEFORE the separator at :595 and restores at :608 so a trailing separator is rejected by backtracking, with the grammar-vs-combinator boundary stated as a design decision at :565-568.

S6 (L S-4, verified incl. the consumer-shape comment) - fuseAll's unrolling makes the right V8 choices for a STATED consumer reason, not a generic speedup claim: leaf.ts:179-273 fully unrolls arity-2 and arity-3 into positional closures with packed-literal result arrays, and the comment at leaf.ts:172 names the target ('the value.js hot shapes - 59 all() sites').

S7 (C S-2, and I re-verified the withdrawal that produced it) - dispatch's Int8Array(128) is exactly minimal and total over its own index domain: leaf.ts:101 `.fill(-1)` gives the sentinel, :137 `ch < 128` closes the read side, :139 `idx >= 0` reads the sign. Table width and index width are the same 128, so at most 128 interned parsers can exist and every index 0..127 is exactly representable - the signed type is load-bearing, not accidental.

S8 (C S-5, verified) - the chain() falsy-seed cure is textbook semver hygiene on a consumer-facing wrong-answer bug: parser.ts:124-137 threads the value unconditionally on success, the retired chainError parameter's removal is justified in-comment by MEASUREMENT ('dead-on-error ... zero callers across value.js + parse-that'), and it landed in a major cut rather than a patch.

S9 (C S-4, verified, with the M3 caveat) - retirement hygiene is machine-enforced and auditable: core.ts:6 and index.ts:10-12 cite the fold row, the deprecating version, the originating finding, the consumer count AND the enforcing gate name, and the gate exists (package.json:34). scripts/proof-no-dead-combinator.mjs goes further than C credits: its vacuity guard at :49-58 proves the grep machinery works before trusting a green, and :63-95 sweeps the SIBLING consumer trees - including ../../value.js/src - to prove zero external consumers before permitting the delete. Cross-repo consumer proof as a precondition for removal is rarer than the citation trail.

S10 (C S-6, verified) - the observable-truth standard, and a gate that documents its own earlier unsoundness: scripts/proof-no-css-surface.mjs:6-14 records that the charter's first draft grepped index.d.ts for CSS substrings, which would have passed GREEN with the CSS parser still shipping because `export *` never inlines them, and rewrites itself to observe the runtime export keys of the bundled dist. Both challenges adopted that standard; so did this re-read.

S11 (MINE, new) - the one place the sideEffects hazard could have become a real `undefined` is closed by the CJS lowering: dist/core.cjs:55-58 emits `whitespace` as an accessor (`Object.defineProperty(exports, "whitespace", { enumerable: true, get: () => packrat.whitespace })`) rather than a value snapshot, so the let-bound export initialised by the top-level _initWhitespace() survives the CommonJS conversion. C-13's breakage half dies here for the require condition, and the ESM half is a live binding by construction.

S12 (MINE, new) - value.js's own consume edge already has what the challenges say parse-that lacks: src/foundation/result.ts:1-6 defines Result<T,E> with `ok`/`err` constructors, and src/css/index.ts:20-21 exports ParseIssue and ParseResult as part of the frozen 52. The JS-boundary invariant O-15 prescribes and B-2/C-14 demand is therefore not a design problem for the receiving side - it has a typed home already built and frozen, one level above wherever a parse-that Parser would ever sit.

But src/parse/parser.ts:711 calls `_initWhitespace()` at module top level, and the built chunk carries it: dist/packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js:657 defines `function _initWhitespace()` and **:1416 calls it bare at top level**. leaf.ts:395-399 shows why it exists — `export let whitespace` is assigned by that call, i.e. a module-level mutation of an exported binding, deliberately deferred to dodge circular-init order. A bundler that takes `sideEffects:false` at its word may drop the statement and leave the exported `whitespace` binding `undefined`. C.S-4 is careful to scope its honesty claim to ansi.ts ("`sideEffects: false` is **honest** for this file") and survives; but neither document checks the package-level declaration, which is the one a consumer's bundler actually reads and the one that licenses the very tree-shaking C.B-2 measures. missed.claim: `package.json` `exports` declares no `"./package.json"` entry, so `require`/`import` of the manifest throws `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` for the tooling that routinely reads it.
missed.proof: Verified: `Object.keys(exports)` → exactly `.`, `./core`, `./diagnostics`, `./packrat`, `./utils`; `exports["./package.json"]` is undefined. Bundler dep-scanners, version probes, and resolver plugins that read a dependency's package.json hit this. It is a one-line packaging fix and it belongs in the same edit as the C.D-5 exports/dts cure. Neither challenge raises it despite both auditing the exports map closely (C.D-5 correctly notes the absence of a `"./*"` wildcard without noticing the manifest is caught by the same absence).

superlatives: S-2 / L.S2 — CONFIRMED BY MY OWN MEASUREMENT. `!process.env.NO_COLOR` (ansi.ts:6) implements the current no-color.org rule exactly on the two edges most implementations miss: I probed `NO_COLOR=""` → `!""` = true, colour stays on (spec: present AND not an empty string) and `NO_COLOR="0"` → `!"0"` = false, colour off (spec: presence, not truthiness). A `"NO_COLOR" in process.env` test over-triggers on the first; a `=== "1"` test fails the second. Both challenges found this independently and both are right.

S-3 / L.S1 — CONFIRMED BY MY OWN MEASUREMENT, and it is the strongest thing in the module. ansi.ts:4-6 orders `typeof process !== "undefined" && process.stderr?.isTTY === true && !process.env.NO_COLOR`. Under the ubiquitous browser shim `process = { env: {} }` I measured the expression → `false`, no throw. Written without the optional chain, the same shim raises `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'isTTY')` — I measured that too — at module-evaluation time inside a top-level `const`, in the shared `packrat-entry` chunk that `core.js:1` imports. That is an unrecoverable boot crash in exactly the browser target the routing law points value.js at. Note the two docs credit different halves: C credits the `?.` on `stderr`, L credits the short-circuit ORDER protecting the unguarded `process.env` read. Both are real and they are independent; the module gets both right.

S-1 — CONFIRMED. Perfect export/consumer parity at the source tier: 10 of 10 exports consumed, by one file, in one import statement (debug.ts:5). My grep for the distinctive symbols outside the pair returns zero third consumers. The contrast C draws is real and verified: index.ts:10-12 documents the fifteen `*Span` builders excised in the 1.0.0 cut as "a zero-consumer surface, deprecated in 0.13.0 (PT-Q4)", policed forever by `proof:no-span-surface` (package.json:46). ansi never accumulated a dead-surface gate because it never needed one.

S-4 / L.S3 / L.S4 — CONFIRMED, and the tree proves the sharp half. ansi.ts has zero import statements; all ten exports are pure `string -> string` top-level arrows with one call signature; the disabled arm is `return s` with no allocation, and the disabled arm is the common arm (I measured `process.stderr.isTTY` → undefined in this session, so vitest/CI/pipes always land there). The proof that the pinning is not ansi's fault is empirical: esbuild DID shake `dim` out of the minified bundle (SGR `2m` count = 0 while the other nine are each 1), so per-symbol elimination works — the nine survivors are held by debug.ts and the class prototypes. This is what makes the §6 relocation cure cheap, and it is the single most useful superlative for the adoption decision.

L.S5 — CONFIRMED. Correct SGR closers rather than the lazy blanket reset: 22 for intensity, 23 for italic, 39 for foreground, 49 for background (ansi.ts:8-17), and `grep '\[0m' src/parse/ansi.ts` → no match. This is what makes `bgRed(bold(" Err x "))` at debug.ts:152 render bold-on-red instead of losing the background at the inner close. C misses this one entirely and in fact reasons wrongly about the same bytes (see killed C.D-8-SGR22) — L is the document to carry forward on ANSI semantics.

L's "On duplication, explicitly" — worth preserving as a ruling, not a superlative: ten near-identical one-liners IS repetition, and L declines to bank a cheap MINOR for it, arguing the `sgr(open, close)` factory would cost a closure frame per helper and defeat constant-folding. missed.claim: all()'s declared tuple type is systematically false: fuseAll drops every `undefined` arm and left-shifts the rest, and arity-1 all() does not build an array at all — so the result's arity and element positions are input-dependent while the type says they are fixed.
missed.proof: NEITHER challenge names this; the C-doc's §3 verdict table (challenge-C-consumption.md:584) rules `all` **KEEP** on "R-LAW-1 rollback exactness by construction", and the L-doc's S-4 (challenge-L-library.md:716-722) praises the unrolled arms without noting they carry the defect. LIVE source: all() is typed `Parser<ExtractValue<T>>` — a positional tuple of arity N (leaf.ts:154-164). Two independent mechanisms break it. (a) DROP-AND-SHIFT: every fuseAll arm guards `if (state.value !== undefined) out[w++] = state.value` (leaf.ts:199, 207 / :230, 238, 246 / :267) and then trims `out.length = w` (:209, :248, :270). (b) ARITY-1 PASSTHROUGH: `parsers.length === 1 ? parsers[0].parser : fuseAll(parsers)` at leaf.ts:161 returns the inner parser's raw value, unwrapped. Witness derived from source: `all(whitespace, string("a"), whitespace)` is typed `Parser<[string,string,string]>`; on "a " the leading whitespace takes regex()'s empty-match arm (leaf.ts:354-357) and yields `undefined`, so w stays 0, string("a") lands at out[0] and the trailing whitespace at out[1] — result `["a", " "]`, arity 2, with the TRAILING whitespace occupying the slot the type says holds the VALUE. `const [ws0, v, ws1] = …` binds v to the whitespace. Same for eof(), which returns `state.ok(undefined)` (leaf.ts:14), in any `all(p, eof())`. The behaviour is deliberate (the comment at leaf.ts:171-176 calls it "the EXACT drop-`undefined` … semantics of the original") but it is stated nowhere on the public signature, and it interacts with B-1: `whitespace` is the single most likely arm to yield `undefined`. After B-1 and B-2 this is the most consumer-dangerous defect on the /core surface, and it is the one an X·P candidate would inherit silently the moment it writes `all(ws, value, ws)`.

missed.claim: regex(r, matchFunction) can move the parse offset BACKWARD to zero, and many()/sepBy()'s zero-width guards do not stop it — an unbounded loop reachable from the published API contract.
missed.proof: D-23 (challenge-L-library.md:638-642) audits the same three lines but files only the shared-`sticky` re-entrancy angle at MINOR with "no current consumer passes a re-entrant matchFunction, so this is latent, not live" — and misses the null-exec path entirely. LIVE source: leaf.ts:337-340. `matchFunction` is typed `(match: RegExpMatchArray | null) => string | null` (leaf.ts:319) — the `null` arm is part of the published signature, so a matchFunction that synthesises a value when the regex misses is an INVITED use, not an abuse. Per spec, a sticky RegExp whose exec() misses resets lastIndex to 0; verified by pure-JS probe: `new RegExp(/\d+/,'y')` with lastIndex=3 on "abcdef" → exec() null, **lastIndex now 0**, so `sticky.lastIndex - savedOffset` = **-3**. Line 340 then calls `state.ok(match, -3)`, and ParserState.ok does `this.offset += offset` (state.ts:56) — the offset jumps backward to 0 with isError false. many()'s only loop guard is `if (state.offset === savedOffset) break;` (parser.ts:538), which a BACKWARD move does not trip, so `regex(r, fn).many()` re-parses from offset 0 forever. sepBy carries the identical guard (parser.ts:605). No depth bound, no iteration cap (many's `max` defaults to Infinity, parser.ts:523), and no typed error — the process hangs rather than throwing. This is the only unbounded-loop path I found on the surface, and it is reachable without any re-entrancy.

missed.claim: dispatch()'s Int8Array index genuinely overflows above 128 distinct parsers: ≥128 silently unreachable, ≥256 silently mis-dispatched to the wrong parser.
missed.proof: Struck by BOTH challenges on the same non-sequitur (challenge-C-consumption.md:488-501 as C-17′ WITHDRAWN and elevated to superlative S-2 at :633-637; challenge-L-library.md:766-768 as struck claim 3) — see killed K-1/K-1b. LIVE source: leaf.ts:104-111 mints an index per distinct **parser**, called at :114 for every entry BEFORE any key write; leaf.ts:101 stores those indices in an `Int8Array(128)`; leaf.ts:139 tests `idx >= 0`. Since keys may be multi-char char-sets (JSDoc, leaf.ts:87) or ranges, entry count is unbounded by the 128 addressable slots. Pure-JS replication of leaf.ts:100-125 with 130 distinct parsers under distinct 2-char ASCII keys: 130 indices minted; `Int8Array` stores 128 as **-128** and 256 as **0**; 4 slots in that table held a wrapped negative index — a parser registered by the consumer, silently unreachable, with leaf.ts:128-132's label still advertising its characters. At ≥256 distinct parsers the wrap reaches valid indices and the dispatcher routes to the WRONG parser with no error. Reachability is bounded (needs >128 distinct parsers in one table with overlapping or multi-char keys), which is why I file MAJOR rather than BLOCKER — but this is exactly the aliasing class getCijKey fail-louds on with a RangeError 300 lines away (packrat.ts:90-98, the L-doc's own S-2), handled the opposite way in the same package. The false 'provably total' superlative is the more damaging artifact: it would license a future candidate to build an unbounded head-dispatch table on this primitive.

missed.claim: dispatch()'s range syntax silently captures unintended characters — including the exact CSS numeric-head key set — and the 6-char two-range form silently degrades to a per-char set.
missed.proof: D-13 (challenge-L-library.md:474-495) audits the >127 key-side OOB and C-17 (challenge-C-consumption.md:471-484) the ASCII bound, but neither examines the range GRAMMAR itself. LIVE source: leaf.ts:116-119 — `if (chars.length === 3 && chars[1] === '-')` reinterprets ANY 3-char key with a middle hyphen as a range `lo..hi`, with no escape and no validation. Verified by pure-JS replication of leaf.ts:113-125: the natural CSS key `"+-."` (plus / minus / dot — the numeric-head set an X·P candidate would write first) satisfies the test and registers the range '+'(43)..'.'(46) = **`+ , - .`**, silently routing `,` into the number parser. Conversely `"0-9a-z"` has length 6, fails the test, and falls to the per-char loop at :121-123, registering exactly `0 - 9 a z` — so `1..8` and `b..y` never dispatch, again silently. The pre-computed label at leaf.ts:128-132 renders the RANGE interpretation (`'+'-'.'`), so the diagnostic agrees with the wrong reading rather than exposing it. `Record<string, Parser<T>>` (leaf.ts:100) accepts all of it, and there is no construction-time check — the posture the same package takes for its own budget overflow at packrat.ts:90-98.

missed.claim: The library has no typed error surface at all: two throw sites in 2,547 lines, no Error subclass, and therefore no failure a consumer can discriminate on.
missed.proof: Both challenges hit fragments of this (D-15 / C-14 on the raw TypeError; C-4 on the missing label; B-2 on the missing Result) but neither states it as one whole-surface property, which is the shape a consumer's boundary invariant has to be written against. LIVE: `grep "throw " src/parse/*.ts` returns exactly TWO sites in the entire tree — packrat.ts:94 (`RangeError`, the memo-budget guard) and debug.ts:337 (a bare `Error`, "parserPrint: missing parser context name"). `grep "class .*Error"` returns NONE. Consequence: the memo-budget overflow, the debug-context invariant violation, and the non-string-input crash (D-15) are mutually indistinguishable from unrelated host errors — no `instanceof` discriminant exists. Combined with B-2 (a failed parse throws nothing, returns a plausible value, and reports only through a per-instance mutable `parser.state.isError` shared across every parse of that grammar), the library offers a consumer exactly ZERO type-safe failure channels. This is the finding a JS-boundary invariant above parse-that must be sized against: it cannot be a try/catch, because the shipping failure mode is not an exception.

missed.claim: Parser.map(fn, mapError = true) converts a failed parse into a success and hands fn the error-state's stale value.
missed.proof: Absent from both challenges. LIVE: parser.ts:146-154 — `const map = (state) => { this.parser(state); if (!state.isError || mapError) { return state.ok(fn(state.value as T)); } return state; }`. `ParserState.ok` clears the flag (`this.isError = false`, state.ts:58). So with mapError set, a failing inner parser yields isError === false; the offset is NOT restored to any checkpoint (unlike opt() at parser.ts:239-241 or not() at :258-260, both of which restore savedOffset before succeeding); and `fn` is invoked on whatever `state.value` the failed inner left behind — frequently a stale value from a prior arm, the same aliasing B-2 exposes at parser.ts:74. The parameter name promises 'map the error'; the behaviour is 'swallow the error and mis-position'. No JSDoc, no test, and no in-tree caller passes it, which is why I file MINOR — but it is public, defaulted-off surface reachable from core.ts:7 with a name that actively misdescribes it.

superlatives: SUP-1 (confirms L-doc S-1 at the bytes) — the zero-allocation result discipline is real and uniformly enforced. I read every combinator in parser.ts (24 of them) and every leaf in leaf.ts (5) and not one returns a freshly-constructed ParserState: all thread the single state object with `savedOffset` locals for backtracking, and ParserState.ok/err/from (state.ts:55-73) mutate in place and return `this`. The ONLY `new ParserState` sites in the whole tree are parser.ts:52 (one per top-level parse), parser.ts:61 (one per FAILED top-level parse) and state.ts:102 (clone, whose sole caller is packrat.ts:351). That is two state allocations per parse regardless of grammar depth. The consistency is the achievement — one combinator returning a fresh state would poison the invariant, and none does. arcsecond, parsimmon and parjs all allocate a result object per step; this is a deliberate, uniformly-held divergence.

SUP-2 (confirms L-doc S-2 verbatim) — getCijKey is the model of how to handle a numeric-precision hazard, and it is the yardstick that condemns two of my own missed findings. packrat.ts:52-100 names the SUPERSEDED bug (`id << 32` overflowing int32 at id ≥ 4096, aliasing getCijKey(4096,0) === getCijKey(0,0)), derives the replacement bound from the float64 mantissa (32 + 21 = 53 bits, MEMO_MAX_ID ≈ 2,097,151 at :77), and then FAILS LOUD with a RangeError at the boundary rather than aliasing (:90-98). Hazard named, bound computed, gate installed, history retained in-comment so the next reader cannot re-introduce the shift. This is the standard — which is exactly why M-3 and M-4 sting: the identical silent-aliasing class, 300 lines away in dispatch(), handled the opposite way in the same file.

SUP-3 (confirms C-doc S-1; the single most valuable property of the split) — module-instance identity is preserved across all five subpath entries. Verified at the emitted graph, not asserted: dist/core.js:1, dist/parse.js:1, dist/packrat.js:1 and dist/utils.js:2 all import the SAME packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js; dist/diagnostics.js:1 and dist/utils.js:1 the same diagnostics-DDazRHgl.js. One Parser class, one diagnosticsEnabled, one PACKRAT_ARMED — so `instanceof Parser` holds across subpaths and enableDiagnostics() from /diagnostics really does arm the leaves /core exports. The dual-package hazard that breaks most multi-entry libraries is absent. It is also the ONLY thing the split actually buys (C-6 confirms the payload premise is worth 6.5%), and it is completely ungated: subpath-gate.mjs never asserts it, and a manualChunks change would break every consumer silently. It deserves a gate more than any surface row does.

SUP-4 (confirms L-doc S-3) — the re-entrancy hardening is sound at two levels and preserves its own falsified prior design as a warning. parser.ts:43-48 wraps parseStateInner in try/finally around packratEnter/packratExit; packrat.ts:390-406 wraps growLR's grow loop in a SECOND try/finally restoring the per-head GROWING/HEADS bookkeeping. packratExit's null-guard (packrat.ts:243-244) makes the unarmed path a true no-op rather than a special case bolted on. And packrat.ts:167-172 documents the PT-Q1 regression this replaced — the per-node reset inside memoizeFn that wiped an outer grow's cells — with its exact failure mode. Fixing a re-entrancy bug AND leaving the falsified prior design in the tree as a warning is rare; most libraries delete the evidence with the bug.

SUP-5 (confirms L-doc S-5 / C-doc S-3 verbatim) — the PT-Q5 retraction docblock at leaf.ts:88-98 is the exemplar of consumption-driven design: a shipped 2nd-byte subTable optimisation DELETED because "It had ZERO production consumers — value.js's only dispatch() calls pass NO subTable — so the widening was a no-consumer perf seam gated against a SYNTHETIC corpus no consumer runs", with the re-entry condition stated IN ADVANCE ("If value.js's coordinated Q session measures an on-path win … not before"). Removing one's own optimisation for want of a real consumer is the rarest discipline in a performance-oriented library, and stating the re-entry condition up front makes the retraction auditable rather than silent. Every defect above is a departure from a standard this file already set for itself, 13 lines above dispatch's own two silent-failure modes.

SUP-6 (my own, and it discharges a corpus obligation) — the dist artifact the prototype workspace resolves is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the main checkout's local build, so every dist-level number in both challenges is reproducible against the artifact a candidate would actually import. docs/tranches/V/megatranche/prototypes/css-parser/node_modules/@mkbabb/parse-that/dist carries the same chunk hashes (packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js, diagnostics-DDazRHgl.js) and the same sizes (1,336 / 40,576 / 3,516) as parse-that/typescript/dist. W1 OP-3 (docs/tranches/X/parse-that/waves/W1.md:65) flags that "a workspace reinstall changes @mkbabb/parse-that's dist bytes and therefore every O-15 number" and asks for re-verification at open. That check is now GREEN and was performed without arming any latch — worth carrying forward, because it is the precondition under which O-15's PT-01/PT-03/PT-04/PT-07 cites and the D-03/C-1/C-6 byte accounting remain quotable at all.

SUP-7 (confirms L-doc S-6) — the two classic combinator footguns are both closed, and one carries its rationale. many() guards zero-width matches at parser.ts:538 (`if (state.offset === savedOffset) break;`) — without it a nullable inner parser is an infinite loop. sepBy() checkpoints BEFORE the separator (parser.ts:595, restored at :598 and :608) so a trailing separator is rejected by backtracking past it, with the design decision stated as a grammar-vs-combinator boundary in the doc-comment at parser.ts:565-568. Both are the errors this genre of library routinely ships with. Worth recording that M-2 is precisely the crack in the first of them: the guard tests offset EQUALITY, not non-regression, so it closes the zero-width footgun and leaves the negative-width one open.

killed.claim: L §m-12: "A span whose offset exceeds src.length + lines.length − 1 matches no line" (challenge-L-library.md:739-740).
killed.refutation: Arithmetic wrong. The accumulator at debug.ts:107 is lineEnd = offsetAcc + lines[i].length + 1; summed over all lines that telescopes to exactly src.length + 1 (the per-line +1 reinstates each of the numLines − 1 newlines and adds one phantom). So the loop's final test is span.offset < src.length + 1 — the drop threshold is offset > src.length, not offset > src.length + lines.length − 1. For src = "ab\ncd" (length 5) the doc's threshold says spans at offset 6 are kept; they are dropped. The silent-drop MECHANISM is confirmed; the stated bound is off by lines.length − 2.

killed.claim: C §C-15 mechanism: "A parser whose id is 0 would therefore (a) never be cached and (b) **fail to terminate the lazy recursion at :325**, since !0 is true and the memo write at :322 happens only after print returns" (challenge-C-consumption.md:437-440).

missed.claim: formatAllDiagnostics(diagnostics, src) renders a PROCESS-GLOBAL, cross-source diagnostic buffer against a SINGLE src — so diagnostics collected from one source get rendered against the text of another, with wrong line, wrong caret, and a `found` snippet belonging to neither.

But collectedDiagnostics is a module global (utils.ts:95 `let collectedDiagnostics: Diagnostic[] = []`), accumulated by collectDiagnostic (utils.ts:115) across EVERY parse in the process, and getCollectedDiagnostics() (utils.ts:138) returns the whole array. So the README's own worked example (README.md:230-232, `console.error(formatAllDiagnostics(diagnostics, css))`) is wrong the moment any other source has been parsed with recovery in the same process — including the exact re-entrancy case parse-that cured elsewhere at parser.ts:34-49. missed.claim: .debug(name, recursivePrint=true) on any grammar containing a bare `new Parser(fn)` node converts the PARSE ITSELF into a throw AND permanently leaks debugDepth in one step — and the DOCUMENTED 2-argument call form is what turns recursivePrint on.

Mechanism: debug.ts:358 debugDepth++ -> :361 child parse succeeds -> :363-364 parserPrint(parser) throws (the M-8/C-3 defect) -> :379 debugDepth-- never runs. The reach is the sting: docs/api.md:81 documents debug(name, logger), so a consumer following the published API writes p.debug("A", myLogger), myLogger binds to recursivePrint as a truthy value (C-4, verified: 0 logger invocations), and the recursive print is forced on every step. missed.claim: summarizeLine's unconditional trimEnd() re-bases SHORT lines too, so the caret overruns for any error inside a trailing-whitespace run — with no length precondition at all. B-1 requires a line over 74 characters; this does not.
missed.proof: debug.ts:15 `const trimmed = line.trimEnd();` runs BEFORE the `len <= MAX_LINE_WIDTH` short-circuit at :19, so the returned content is shorter than the source line whenever the line has trailing whitespace, while debug.ts:83 still pads with the raw columnNum. MEASURED against dist: new ParserState("abc      ", undefined, 6, true) renders the content line as " 1 | abc" (8 columns) with the caret at column 11 — three columns past the end of the line it annotates. The overrun equals columnNum − trimmedLen and grows with the depth of the trailing run; a whitespace-only line degenerates to " 1 | " with the caret arbitrarily far right. Reachable on any grammar that fails at end-of-line whitespace — the ordinary shape of a trailing-content or unclosed-delimiter failure. Both challenges attribute ALL caret mis-registration to the >74-char truncation path; this is a second, independent mechanism in the same function.

missed.claim: Tab-indented sources mis-register the caret in the terminal: the content line emits raw tabs while the caret line is built from literal spaces, so the caret is at the right character index and the wrong visual column.

missed.claim: formatDiagnostic renders TWO independently-computed locations for one error inside ONE block, and they disagree precisely in the B-2 case: the header says 1:0 while the caret is drawn on line 2 at column −1.

Two lines later, debug.ts:207 reconstructs `new ParserState(src, undefined, d.furthestOffset, true)` and hands it to addCursor, which RE-COMPUTES the same location through state.getLineAndColumn() (debug.ts:59 -> state.ts:128), the clamped-lastIndexOf algorithm. The rendered document therefore contradicts itself: header and body point at different lines for the same error. This is the concrete consequence of the two implementations NOT being identical, which is what L §B-2's falsifier (b) wrongly asserted they were. Practical reach is currently 0 because formatDiagnostic is exported from no entry (M-1/C-1), the only reason this is MINOR.

confirmed.claim: The non-string boundary is three-valued — throw / silent-reject / silent-ACCEPT — and it is a property of the grammar's first leaf, not of parseState

MEASURED at runtime: `regex(/[0-9]+/).map(Number).not(string("!")).parseState("12").value` → `12`, typeof "number", while the declaration says string — so `p.not(q).parse(s).toUpperCase()` typechecks under strict and crashes. missed.claim: `.trim(p)` silently DISCARDS the parser it is handed, and the library publishes three mutually incompatible whitespace definitions under one name.
missed.proof: parser.ts:488 dispatches on `parser.context?.name === "whitespace"` and takes the inline trimStateWhitespace path (parser.ts:498-517), never invoking the argument. The three classes are all barrel exports: `whitespace` = `regex(/\s*/)` (leaf.ts:397, index.ts:9 — JS `\s`, matches U+00A0/U+FEFF); `trimStateWhitespace` (leaf.ts:383, index.ts:9 — only charCode 32 and 9..13); `skipWhitespace` (utils.ts:162, index.ts:5 — charCode <= 32, so it eats U+0001..U+001F). MEASURED: `string("a").trim(whitespace).parseState(" a ")` → isError=TRUE, while `all(whitespace, string("a"), whitespace).parseState(" a ")` → isError=FALSE — the consumer passes the Unicode-whitespace parser explicitly and gets the ASCII-only scanner. Also `skipWhitespace` advances past U+0001 (offset 1) where `trimStateWhitespace` does not (offset 0). challenge-L·m-10 found the context-name dispatch and scored only the mutation hazard; neither challenge measured the substitution or the three-way divergence.

missed.claim: `regex(r, matchFunction)` can move the offset BACKWARD and report success, and every zero-advance guard in the library is blind to it.
missed.proof: leaf.ts:337-340: `const execResult = sticky.exec(state.src); const match = matchFunction!(execResult); if (match) { return state.ok(match, sticky.lastIndex - savedOffset); }`. Per spec, a failed `exec` on a sticky/global RegExp RESETS lastIndex to 0, so when matchFunction legitimately returns a value for a null match (its parameter is typed `RegExpMatchArray | null` at leaf.ts:319, i.e. the case is designed for) the advance is `0 - savedOffset`, and state.ts:56 `this.offset += offset` lands the parse at offset 0. MEASURED: `string("ab").then(regex(/[0-9]+/, m => m ? m[0] : "FALLBACK")).parseState("abZZ")` → isError=FALSE, **offset=0**, value=["ab","FALLBACK"]. The guards at parser.ts:538 (`many`), :582/:605 (`sepBy`) all test `offset === savedOffset`, never `<`, so a rewind is invisible to them — which is exactly why challenge-L·S-2 could praise those guards and still miss this.

missed.claim: `dispatch()` silently drops every non-ASCII key at construction — an out-of-range typed-array store that is a no-op — while the precomputed error label still advertises the key.
missed.proof: leaf.ts:101 `const tbl = new Int8Array(128).fill(-1)`; leaf.ts:119 and :122 write `tbl[c] = idx` / `tbl[chars.charCodeAt(i)] = idx` with no bound check, so any key whose code is >= 128 writes out of range and is discarded silently. The label is built from `Object.keys(table)` at leaf.ts:128-132 and still names the key. MEASURED: `dispatch({"é": string("é"), "a": string("a")})` parses "a" (isError=false) and REJECTS "é" (isError=true) with label `one of ['é', 'a']`. This is the REACHABLE sibling of challenge-L·m-3 — which honestly rates its own index-wrap arm unreachable with single-char keys — and it is the write-path half of the read path challenge-L·S-5 praises. It also contradicts the fail-loud posture challenge-L·S-1 correctly celebrates in getCijKey (packrat.ts:90-97), in the same file's own idiom.

missed.claim: `csvParser` does not split rows — a published, eagerly-constructed export that contradicts its own doc comment.
missed.proof: parsers/csv.ts:11-20: `token = any(regex(/[^"]+/).wrap(…), regex(/[^']+/).wrap(…), regex(/[^,]+/))` — the unquoted arm `[^,]+` matches newlines — then `line = token.sepBy(delim).trim()` and `csvParser = line.many()`. There is no row separator anywhere in the grammar. MEASURED: `csvParser.parse("a,b\nc,d")` → `[["a","b\nc","d"]]` — ONE row, with the newline swallowed into a field; csv.ts:19 says "returns array of rows, each an array of string fields". This is one of the 36 parsers the barrel mints eagerly at import (challenge-L·M-1) and one of the two module singletons that pin their input forever (challenge-L·M-10); both challenges read parsers/csv.ts whole, scored it as a "showcase", and never ran it.

missed.claim: `mapState`'s `oldState` is a live prototype view, not a snapshot: only offset and value are old, every other field reads the NEW state through the prototype chain.
missed.proof: parser.ts:177-179 `const oldView = Object.create(state); oldView.offset = oldOffset; oldView.value = oldValue;` then `fn(state, oldView)`. MEASURED inside a real callback: `Object.getPrototypeOf(oldState) === newState` → TRUE and `Object.keys(oldState)` → `["offset","value"]`. So `oldState.isError`, `.src`, `.furthest`, `.expected`, `.suggestions`, `.secondarySpans` are all the post-parse values, while the parameter is named oldState and typed `ParserState<T>` (dist/parser.d.ts:17). Secondary cost inside this seat's lens: every invocation mints an object whose prototype is a DISTINCT ParserState instance, so the callback's property-access sites are megamorphic by construction — the precise hazard challenge-L·S-4 went looking for on ParserState and correctly cleared, one method away.

missed.claim: all()/many()/sepBy() hand back arrays whose V8 elements kind depends on arity — the unrolled arms return PACKED, the pre-sized general arms return HOLEY.
missed.proof: leaf.ts:257 (`const out: unknown[] = new Array(n)`) and parser.ts:526/:572 (`new Array<T>(est)`) create holey arrays that stay holey after being filled; leaf.ts:191 and :222 use array literals (`[undefined, undefined]`, `[undefined, undefined, undefined]`) which are packed. MEASURED with `node --allow-natives-syntax` + `%DebugPrint`: `all(a,b,c,d).parse("abcd")` → `elements kind: HOLEY_ELEMENTS`; `all(a,b,c).parse("abc")` → `PACKED_ELEMENTS`; `string("a").many(3).parse("aaa")` → `HOLEY_ELEMENTS`. The fusion design note at leaf.ts:172-174 justifies the unrolling so "V8 sees a monomorphic call site with constant-folded parser bindings" — but the deliverable it hands the CONSUMER is polymorphic across arities, and the consumer's loops are where the megamorphism actually lands. Directly qualifies challenge-L·S-6, which praises the unrolling and the pre-sized general arm in the same breath.

missed.claim: `quotedString(quote)` interpolates its delimiter into a RegExp character class unescaped.
missed.proof: parsers/utils.ts:16 `const inner = regex(new RegExp(`[^${quote}\\\\]+`)).or(escapedString());` with `quote: string = '"'` — a plain string parameter, no escaping, no length check. MEASURED: `quotedString("]")` compiles to `/[^]\]+/` (i.e. `[^]` = any character, then a literal `\]`) and REJECTS `"]a]"` (isError=true) where the intended parse succeeds. `-`, `]`, `\` and any multi-character argument mis-compile silently. Published from the barrel via index.ts:14 → parsers/index.ts:8 and from ./utils (utils-entry.ts:10-14). Both challenges list `quotedString` among the RETIRE set on grounds of scope and neither exercised it.

missed.claim: `eof<T>()` is a second phantom generic on the published surface — the type parameter appears nowhere in the signature.
missed.proof: leaf.ts:11 `export function eof<T>()` whose body is typed over `ParserState<T>` but which returns `makeParser(...) as Parser<unknown>` (leaf.ts:21-24). SHIPPED: dist/leaf.d.ts:3 `export declare function eof<T>(): Parser<unknown>;` — T is unreferenced, so `eof<number>()` and `eof<string>()` are the same call and both yield `Parser<unknown>`. challenge-L·M-11 names only `ParserFunction<T>` as the package's phantom generic and calls it "a public exported type that reads as a typed function pointer and carries zero type information"; the same defect sits on a leaf combinator the barrel publishes at index.ts:9.

superlatives: L·S-1 CONFIRMED, and the arithmetic is exact — getCijKey's float64 key budget is genuinely right. packrat.ts:71-77 chooses MEMO_OFFSET_SPAN = 2^32 and MEMO_MAX_ID = floor(MAX_SAFE_INTEGER / 2^32) = 2,097,151; the worst-case key 2097151 × 2^32 + (2^32 − 1) = 9,007,199,254,740,991 = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER EXACTLY — the bound is tight, not conservative-by-luck. The offset is added whole (no mask), the boundary is a thrown RangeError with a rationale (packrat.ts:90-98), and `grep -n getCijKey src/parse/packrat.ts` shows it is the sole key constructor with both call sites (:306, :437) behind the guard. Better than the same file's own dispatch (m-3, and the missed non-ASCII row).

L·S-2 CONFIRMED — zero-advance guards make empty-matching parsers non-looping. parser.ts:538 (`if (state.offset === savedOffset) break`), :582 (`else if (state.offset !== savedOffset)`), :605 (`if (state.isError || state.offset === savedOffset)`), and `many`/`sepBy` are the only two repetition combinators, both iterative rather than recursive, so neither contributes to the PT-04 stack ceiling. `string("")` (leaf.ts:296-297, `startsWith("", off)` always true) and `regex(/\s*/)` (leaf.ts:354-357) are both constructible from the barrel and neither can hang. QUALIFIED, not diminished, by the missed backward-offset row: the guards test `===`, never `<`.

L·S-3 CONFIRMED — the packrat re-entrancy unwind is genuinely sound and growLR's "no count cap needed" claim verifies. parser.ts:43-48 opens the epoch in a try and restores it in finally; packrat.ts:390-406 does the same for per-head GROWING/HEADS. growLR's `while (true)` (:392) breaks at :398 on `ans.isError || ans.offset <= seed.offset`, seeds advance strictly monotonically, offsets are bounded by src.length — the loop is bounded by input length, exactly as packrat.ts:50 asserts. A throw anywhere discards the child's tables wholesale rather than leaving them on the parent's stack.

L·S-4 CONFIRMED by measurement, not inference — ParserState's object shape is stable and the V8 hazard is absent. state.ts:43 declares `expected?: string[]` with no initialiser, which under a pre-ES2022 emit would leave the property absent until mergeErrorState's first write; tsconfig.json:3 sets target ES2022 so useDefineForClassFields defaults on. MEASURED: `Object.keys(new ParserState("abc"))` → ['expected','suggestions','secondarySpans','src','value','offset','isError','furthest'] — all eight, fixed order, one shape, no transition on first error.

L·S-5 CONFIRMED — dispatch()'s two obvious bugs are both absent, and non-obviously so. killed.claim: "I traced both across the newline/no-newline cases and they are semantically identical (`src.slice(0,furthest).lastIndexOf("\n")` ≡ `src.lastIndexOf("\n", furthest-1)`)… The fork is gratuitous" (challenge-L-library.md:167), and cure #6: "Delete `utils.ts:106-110` in favor of `state.getLineAndColumn`" (challenge-L-library.md:474).

But `src.lastIndexOf("\n", -1)` clamps its position argument to `min(max(-1,0),len) = 0` and therefore **matches** the newline at index 0 → `state.ts:129-132` gives `{line:2, column:-1}`. Applying L-doc cure #6 would inject that bug into every collected `Diagnostic` — a negative column and an off-by-one line on any source beginning with a newline. The corpus contains its own refutation: challenge-C-consumption.md:767-777 (S-5) credits `collectDiagnostic` as "correct where the shared helper is not" and measures the same three cases. The correct cure is the inverse of the one prescribed: install `collectDiagnostic`'s slice-first algorithm INTO `state.getLineAndColumn`, and fix the split-to-count at both sites.
