").length` — the slice EXCLUDES the matched newline — while `state.ts:129-131` computes `slice(0, lastNewline + 1)` — INCLUDING it. The two shifts (inclusive `offset` vs `offset-1`, exclusive vs inclusive slice) cancel exactly when `src[offset] === "
"`. Worked on the live bytes: `src="a
b"`, `offset=1` → `getLineNumber()`: `lastIndexOf("
",1)=1`, `slice(0,1)="a"` → **1**; `getLineAndColumn(1)`: `lastIndexOf("
",0)=-1` → line **1**. Equal. killed.claim: "REFUTED — 'the unarmed suggestions/secondarySpans clears are a hot-path allocation cost'… pre-GC churn: 0.3 MiB (~0.16 bytes/reject); post-GC retained: 0.03 MiB → churn, not leak. V8's young generation absorbs it entirely. **NOT a defect.**" (challenge-C-consumption.md:671-689)

confirmed.claim: Dual-package hazard on a module whose state is 100% global: ESM and CJS get two flags and two buffers.

confirmed.claim: Diagnostic is structurally non-conformant with the frozen ParseIssue on all five EQ-4 fields; no total information-preserving map exists.

confirmed.claim: ParserState.getLineAndColumn is wrong at offset 0 on a leading-newline source — {line:2, column:-1} where the answer is {line:1, column:0} — and collectDiagnostic's fork is the correct one.
confirmed.proof:
CONFIRMED analytically from the spec, no execution needed. state.ts:128 does `src.lastIndexOf("
", offset - 1)`; at offset 0 the position argument -1 is clamped to 0 by String.prototype.lastIndexOf, so on src starting with

").length = 2, column = 0 - 0 - 1 = -1. collectDiagnostic (utils.ts:107-110) slices FIRST — `before = src.slice(0,0)` = "" → lastIndexOf = -1 → line 1, column 0 — sidestepping the clamping trap entirely. The broken method is public on both the root barrel (index.ts:3) and /core (core.ts:9), and sits on the armed console.error path (debug.ts:59 → statePrint → toString), so C·B-2's aggravation limb ('the sole effect enableDiagnostics buys can print a negative column') is CONFIRMED. Only two callers of getLineAndColumn exist package-wide: state.ts:127 (definition) and debug.ts:59 (uncompensated). This finding is load-bearing for K2 below.

confirmed.claim: Diagnostic.found is a lossy presentation string and the shape's only byte-level record: 20-char clamp, escaping transform, no extent field, UTF-16 slicing, one-character escape list, and a fresh RegExp per call.

Escaping: \r, \t, \x1b and every other C0 control pass through untouched into a string the library itself renders inside ANSI context at debug.ts:224-225 — formatDiagnostic (debug.ts:200-229) applies no sanitizer. Against W2's COMP-1 (:241-244) and R-LAW-2 (:279-280) — 'Bytes skipped by recovery enter C; they never vanish' — the skipped bytes are recorded ONLY as this clamped, escaped 20-char prefix; the complement cannot be reconstructed and there is no carrier for either law.

killed.id: C·D-11 (consequence) + C·§5 WRAP limb (a) + L·B-4 limb 1
killed.claim: C·D-11: 'The save/restore posture every well-behaved library wants … is unavailable. A consumer arming diagnostics must clobber its caller's posture' and, decisively, 'it means W1's G-5 cannot be asserted from outside the package — the harness can only refrain from calling enableDiagnostics; it cannot verify the state … That is a weaker gate than W1 believes it has.' killed.refutation: FALSE, and this is the pass's most consequential kill. The flag IS observable through published exports alone, purely, with zero side effects. utils.ts:33 is `state.expected = diagnosticsEnabled && label ? [label] : undefined` — with `label` a non-empty constant the ternary condition is EXACTLY diagnosticsEnabled, so on a fresh throwaway state (offset 0 > furthest -1, taking the :29 branch) `state.expected !== undefined` ⟺ the flag is armed. Three published lines: `const s = new ParserState("", undefined, 0, false, -1)` (ParserState from /core:9 or index.ts:3); `mergeErrorState(s, "probe")` (from /diagnostics:7 or index.ts:5); `return s.expected !== undefined`. RUN LIVE this session in the prototypes workspace against @mkbabb/parse-that@1.0.0, arming nothing and running no bench: 'published-surface flag read (nothing armed): false' and 'journal untouched, len = 0'. mergeErrorState writes only the state passed in (C·S-4/L·S-2, independently verified), so the probe cannot perturb a live parse or the journal. What survives: the REACHABILITY claim (isDiagnosticsEnabled is exported from no entry — utils.ts:16, dist/utils.d.ts:5, chunk alias `i` at :119) is CONFIRMED, and having to hand-roll a probe is a genuine ergonomics defect. killed.claim: 'Duplication is unambiguous — I traced both across the newline/no-newline cases and they are semantically identical (src.slice(0,furthest).lastIndexOf("\n") ≡ src.lastIndexOf("\n", furthest-1))'; cure §8.6: 'Delete utils.ts:106-110 in favor of state.getLineAndColumn.'

The equivalence is FALSE and the cure is REGRESSIVE — refuted by the sibling document's own C·D-14/C·S-5, which the L pass did not read. At furthest = 0 on a leading-newline source the two diverge: `"
…".slice(0,0).lastIndexOf("
")` = -1 (correct → line 1, column 0), while `"
…".lastIndexOf("
", -1)` clamps its position argument to 0 and MATCHES index 0 (→ line 2, column -1). Applying L·M-2's cure would install a negative column and an off-by-one line into every collected Diagnostic at offset 0 of any source beginning with a newline — a class CSS grammars hit constantly (leading blank line in a stylesheet). What survives: the duplication is real, the fork is undesirable, and the surviving allocation limb (`.split("
").length` as a split-to-count, utils.ts:109 and state.ts:131) is CONFIRMED. Correct cure, which neither doc states: fix state.ts:128 first (clamp-safe: `offset > 0 ? src.lastIndexOf("
", offset - 1) : -1`), THEN unify — never the reverse. The L doc's §8 item 6 orders it the reverse way.

killed.claim: L·M-1: 'MAJOR (hot-path allocation) … A 100-char CSS value can burn ~200 short-lived array allocations per parse … this is not noise in the budget of a hot parser library.' C·INFO-A: 'REFUTED … NOT a defect', evidenced by 'pre-GC churn: 0.3 MiB (~0.16 bytes/reject); post-GC retained: 0.03 MiB'.
killed.refutation: BOTH wrong; the true answer is between them. The MECHANISM is CONFIRMED — utils.ts:33 is gated and :34-35 are not, in the same function, adjacent statements, and with the flag off the only writers (addSuggestion :52-54, addSecondarySpan :58-60) are both guarded, so the two arrays are provably dead. But L·M-1's MAJOR over-rates it: 2 young-gen array allocations per NEW-FURTHEST event, bounded by distinct offsets reached, at a few ns each. And C·INFO-A's refutation is methodologically unsound: a `heapUsed` delta across a 2,000,000-iteration loop measures RETENTION, not allocation rate — scavenges during the loop erase churn from the reading entirely, so 0.3 MiB cannot support 'V8's young generation absorbs it entirely'; it only supports 'not a leak', which was never the claim. Allocation cost is visible in TIME, not in heapUsed. Correct disposition: MINOR, cure is one line (hoist :34-35 inside the existing :33 flag test), and the real measurement is MEASURE-AT-OPEN on the DEBT-2 reject leg (parser-band.md:117). I also correct L·M-1's arithmetic: it lists '20 call sites' and enumerates leaf.ts ×4, but grep gives 22 call sites (leaf.ts:16,54,69,142,291,303,360 = 7 and parser.ts ×15); its own enumeration silently drops leaf.ts:291/:303/:360. L·M-9's falsifier repeats the same '20 sites' figure.

killed.id: C·D-14 ('three conventions') + C·§5 WRAP limb (b) + L·M-11 severity
killed.claim: C·D-14: 'three mutually inconsistent line conventions ship in one library'. C·§5: the WRAP column is empty because '(b) scope the journal per parse — impossible, recover() writes the global directly and unguarded'. L·M-11: MAJOR — 'the subpath is not self-contained in TypeScript'.

MINOR.

missed.claim: MISSED-1 — value.js's frozen ParseResult<T> forbids diagnostics on SUCCESS (`diagnostics: readonly []`), so recover()'s entire product — partial success carrying N diagnostics — is UNREPRESENTABLE in the /css contract. Both passes analyse only the failure arm.
missed.proof: value.js/src/css/types.ts:25-27 read whole: the success arm is `{ readonly ok: true; readonly value: T; readonly diagnostics: readonly [] }` — an EMPTY TUPLE, not `readonly ParseIssue[]`. parse-that's recover() returns `state.ok(sentinel)` at parser.ts:681, i.e. isError = false, WITH one Diagnostic already pushed at :666 and deliberately not popped. That exact shape is asserted green in value.js's own GROUND-B suite: prototypes/css-parser/idiom/example.test.ts:251-264 — `expect(state.isError).toBe(false)` alongside `expect(diagnostics.length).toBe(1)` on input '(1px, ?, 3)'. So the tier's flagship capability produces a value the frozen contract has no arm for: at adoption the wave must either discard diagnostics on success, or flip ok:false on a parse that succeeded, or reopen the frozen contract. C·D-7 discusses only the failure arm's non-emptiness; W2.md:292-295 likewise holds only `{ok:false; diagnostics: readonly [ParseIssue, ...ParseIssue[]]}` load-bearing and never states the dual. Neither challenge doc contains the string `readonly []`, 'success arm', or 'ok: true' (grepped). This is the sharpest consumption consequence of the collection tier for the parser wave and it strengthens the RETIRE verdict on a ground §5 never reaches.

missed.claim: MISSED-2 — R-LAW-5 is the ONE recovery law that names `recover` explicitly, and it appears ZERO times in either challenge document. Live, parse-that violates its declaration requirement: a recovered non-final alternative silently starves every later arm, and nothing in the library declares it.
missed.proof: `grep -c 'R-LAW-5'` over both challenge docs → 0 and 0. W2.md:287-290 reads: 'R-LAW-5 — the alt/recover interaction, declared. A recovered branch is a SUCCESS for the enclosing choice, so a first arm that recovers starves the second. The contract states the rule (forbid recovery inside a non-final choice arm, or declare the alternative) — leaving it undeclared is how a lenient parser silently stops being total.' Live mechanism verified: recover returns `state.ok(sentinel)` (parser.ts:681) which sets isError = false (state.ts:55-60); `any` returns on the FIRST non-error arm and never tries the rest (leaf.ts:61-68, and the 2-arity fast path at :42-57 identically). The library declares nothing: README §Error Recovery (:210-239) is silent on the alt interaction; diagnostics.ts:1-5 documents the tier, not the protocol; and `.recover(` appears NOWHERE in src/, test/ or scripts/ outside its definition, so there is not even a test pinning the behaviour. This lands directly on the band: both cand-O (cand-o/grammar.ts:38) and cand-F (cand-f/color.ts:66) are any/dispatch-shaped grammars (parser-band.md:108), so any wave that adopts recover() to discharge DEBT-1 inherits an undeclared totality hazard on the very combinator that is this module's sole producer.

missed.claim: MISSED-3 — core.ts's isolation comment is false on TWO of its three limbs, not one. Both L·M-8 and C·D-17 charge only the diagnostics limb; the packrat limb is equally false, and only the json/csv limb holds.
missed.proof: src/parse/core.ts:4-5 promises a consumer 'never pulls the diagnostics accumulator, THE PACKRAT TIER, or the json/csv domain parsers.' The runtime chunk that dist/core.js:1 imports IS `packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js` — literally the packrat entry — and `grep -c 'PACKRAT_ARMED|packratEnter'` in it returns 6 (the latch at :678, its reads at :682/:714, its write at :722, plus the enter/exit functions), because parser.ts:7 hard-imports packratEnter/packratExit and parser.ts:43-47 calls them in a try/finally on every parseState. So /core loads the packrat tier's module and its one-way latch too — unarmed, but present and one makeMemoized() away from arming. The third limb is the only true one: `grep -c 'jsonParser|csvParser'` returns 0 in both packrat-entry-CS1td-8B.js and core.js. Sharpening matters for the wave's disposition: the subpath split buys a consumer NOTHING architecturally — it is cosmetic on two of three axes — which is an independent argument for retiring the boundary rather than porting it.

missed.claim: MISSED-4 — W1's G-5 quarantine can be asserted DIRECTLY from outside the package, upgrading it from a byte-empty-stderr proxy to a positive assertion. This is the constructive half of the K1 kill and neither pass found it.
missed.proof: G-5 as written (W1.md:465-466, GREEN condition :481-494) proves 'no cell ran armed' only indirectly — by observing that stderr is byte-empty — and C·D-11 concluded the direct assertion is impossible. It is not. Three published lines, verified live this session against @mkbabb/parse-that@1.0.0 with nothing armed: `const s = new ParserState('', undefined, 0, false, -1); mergeErrorState(s, 'probe'); return s.expected !== undefined;` → printed `false`, with the journal untouched at length 0. ParserState comes from /core (core.ts:9) or root (index.ts:3); mergeErrorState from /diagnostics (diagnostics.ts:7) or root (index.ts:5). The equivalence is exact by construction at utils.ts:33 and needs no arming to establish. Recommended G-5 amendment: assert this predicate `=== false` at bench-cell ENTRY and EXIT, the same shape G-4 already uses for PACKRAT_ARMED (W1.md:460-463) — which closes the hole C·D-11 correctly identified (a transitive dependency that arms defeats the quarantine silently) rather than merely naming it.

superlatives: LIVE-S-1 (NEW, neither pass credits it) — `many()` already satisfies R-LAW-4's progress clause by construction. parser.ts:538 `if (state.offset === savedOffset) break;` sits immediately after the success branch, so a zero-width `sync` inside `.many().recover(...)` breaks the loop instead of spinning. I formed the hypothesis that recover + a zero-width sync hangs the documented `many()/sepBy()` idiom (parser.ts:650-651) — W2.md:284-286 makes exactly that a probe ('a lowering that hangs or emits N² fails') — and KILLED IT AGAINST MYSELF at :538. The guard predates the diagnostics tier and is the reason the library's headline recovery idiom is safe at all. Residual, folded not filed: with a zero-width sync the loop truncates silently at the first recovery while the diagnostic for that element stays in the global buffer — an R-LAW-4 UNDER-count, requiring a grammar bug to reach.

LIVE-S-2 (NEW) — the flag the library refuses to export is nonetheless observable, purely, through two published symbols. utils.ts:33's ternary condition is exactly `diagnosticsEnabled` when `label` is a non-empty constant, and mergeErrorState writes only the state handed to it, so a throwaway ParserState is a side-effect-free reader. Withholding isDiagnosticsEnabled (utils.ts:16) was an ergonomics mistake, not a capability loss — and the accident that leaves the reader intact is what rescues W1's G-5 from resting on a stderr proxy. Verified live, unarmed: read returns false, journal length 0.

LIVE-S-3 (NEW) — value.js's own /css contract is the asset, and it is strictly better than anything parse-that can produce. src/css/types.ts:25-27 makes the success arm carry `readonly []` and the failure arm a non-empty tuple `readonly [ParseIssue, ...ParseIssue[]]`, with ParseIssue (:10-24) deep-Readonly over a closed 8-code union and start/end SPANS rather than points. That single type forbids PT-07's undefined-on-failure at the type level, forbids the hollow-diagnostic posture C·B-4 measures, and forbids the two-position drift C·D-12 finds in Diagnostic — before any code is written. The nine entry points already honour it (timeline.ts:17,:66; grammar.ts:257,:334,:393,:397,:405,:436; stylesheet.ts:743). RETIRE is right not because parse-that's tier is bad in isolation but because the consumer already holds the better algebra.

L·S-1 / C·S-6 RE-VERIFIED — /diagnostics is a true runtime leaf: 125 lines, 3,516 bytes, zero import statements in dist/diagnostics-DDazRHgl.js. Held only by discipline — utils.ts:1 and :3 are `import type` / `export type` under verbatimModuleSyntax (tsconfig.json:8); one value import from state.js would drag debug + ansi into every consumer of the toggles (state.ts:2 imports statePrint). Verified in the published artifact, not inferred.

confirmed.claim: `getLazyParser`'s `undefined` sentinel conflates "not cached" with "cached `undefined`".

The only prose is the inline "Build a lightweight view for the old state" (parser.ts:176). It is reachable from `index.ts:2` as a method on the exported class and has ZERO callers and ZERO tests: `grep -rn mapState src/ test/ scripts/` returns only parser.ts:162/168/184/185 and the `parserNames` entry at state.ts:167. missed.claim: The published `lazy` decorator's own doc comment is false — it caches nothing across calls — and it binds `this` to the prototype rather than the instance.

But lazy.ts:37-42 replaces `descriptor.value` with `function () { return new Parser(createLazyCached(method), createParserContext("lazy", undefined, method)); }` — `createLazyCached` is invoked **inside** the replacement, so every call to the decorated method mints a fresh closure with a fresh `let cached` slot (lazy.ts:19) and a fresh `new Parser`. Separately, lazy.ts:35 does `descriptor.value!.bind(target)`, and for an instance-method decorator `target` is the **prototype**, so the decorated method's `this` is the prototype and any instance state is invisible to the grammar it builds. Both are dead today (`grep -rn '@lazy' src test` → empty), which is why this is MINOR — but it compounds C-M9 into a three-way defect on the barrel's most-expected name (index.ts:7): a decorator that cannot compile under the package's own tsconfig, does not cache what its doc comment says it caches, and binds `this` wrong.

Live leaf.ts:116 `if (chars.length === 3 && chars[1] === '-')` decides range-vs-literal, and the label builder repeats the identical test at leaf.ts:129. Two consequences, neither validated and neither documented. (a) A 3-character key whose middle character is `-` is ALWAYS a range, so there is **no way to register the literal characters `a`, `-`, `b` in one key** — `dispatch({"a-b": p})` registers the span. json.ts:44-45 works only because `"-"` is length 1. (b) A key like `"a-zA-Z"` (length 6) silently falls to the multi-char branch (leaf.ts:121-123) and registers the literal set {a,-,z,A,Z}; every other letter then falls to the labelled error arm (leaf.ts:142-144), and the precomputed label (leaf.ts:128-132) reports `one of ['a', '-', 'z', 'A', '-', 'Z']` — so the error message documents the misparse as if it were the intent. superlatives: MISSED SUPERLATIVE — `.fill(-1)` at leaf.ts:101 is the third absent `dispatch()` bug, and it is the one that makes the other two safe. `const tbl = new Int8Array(128).fill(-1);` establishes a NEGATIVE sentinel for every unregistered code point, which is what makes `const idx = ch < 128 ? tbl[ch] : -1; if (idx >= 0)` (leaf.ts:137-139) correct. Without it a fresh `Int8Array` is all zeros, so every unregistered ASCII character would read `tbl[c] === 0`, pass the guard, and dispatch to `parsers[0]` — a silent mis-dispatch of the entire unregistered alphabet to whichever parser happened to intern first, and a wrong answer with no error. It is also what completes L:S-5's EOF/non-ASCII analysis: the `NaN < 128` fall-through and the `-1` sentinel meet at the same comparison. Neither file scores it, and L:m-3 quotes this exact line with the `.fill(-1)` removed while arguing that the same function lacks a guard.

MISSED SUPERLATIVE — `sepBy`'s pre-separator checkpoint gets the trailing-separator problem right in both directions, which most combinator libraries do not. parser.ts:594-611: the loop snapshots `cpBeforeSep = state.offset` BEFORE running the separator, and rewinds to it when either the separator fails (:597-600) or the following element fails or fails to advance (:605-610). The contract is stated in the doc comment (parser.ts:565-568, "Never accepts a trailing separator — trailing sep acceptance is a grammar concern") and the mechanism is stated at the two rewind sites (:592-593, :606-607). superlatives: `string()`'s single-char fast path is the best code in the module — leaf.ts:282-294. One `charCodeAt` compare, and on success it stores the shared `str` reference (`state.unsafeSetValue(str)`, :287), not a fresh substring. Zero allocation on the hottest leaf in any grammar, where most combinator libraries pay a string per token. CONFIRMED by reading every path.

`regex()` chooses `test()` over `exec()` on the default path — leaf.ts:344-347 — genuinely avoiding the `RegExpMatchArray` allocation, and falls back to `exec()` only when a `matchFunction` needs the full array (:335-338). The header's "zero-alloc" overclaims by one `substring` (:350), but the decision is right and is the largest allocation win in the file.

`trimStateWhitespace` is exemplary — leaf.ts:372-391. Zero allocation, no regex-engine entry, a correct fast-exit at :378 that dodges loop setup for the overwhelmingly common non-whitespace case, and an explicit code-point comment at :382 rather than a magic predicate. Its only sin is being one of three alphabets; the code itself is right.

`any()` and `dispatch()` allocate nothing per invocation — verified by reading every path: `any` (leaf.ts:42-72) holds one integer, `dispatch` (:134-145) holds two. For a module whose job is alternation, the classic allocation sink in combinator libraries, this is sustained discipline.

`dispatch()`'s `Int8Array(128).fill(-1)` is the right data structure — leaf.ts:101. 128 bytes, O(1), no Map, no hashing, and the `-1` fill correctly frees index 0 for a real parser. The width is the bug; the design is not.

`dispatch()`'s end-of-input handling is exactly right and free — leaf.ts:136-137. Past the end `charCodeAt` yields NaN, `NaN < 128` is false, the expression falls to -1 and takes the labelled error path. The guard that keeps non-ASCII out of a 128-entry table IS the EOF guard: one comparison doing two jobs, no bounds check, no special case.

The zero-width leaves are safe by construction — `string("")` (leaf.ts:296-306, measured: isError false / value "" / offset 0, succeeding at EOF where `regex(/\s*/)` does not) and regex's empty-match arm (:354-357) both leave `offset` untouched, and every looping combinator upstream guards on `state.offset === savedOffset` (parser.ts:538, 582, 605). The leaf supports the `succeed`-from-`string("")` idiom correctly and deliberately.

Every label in the library is a construction-time constant — leaf.ts:127-132, :278, :324, all evaluated in the factory body above the returned closure. Zero string allocation on the error path; the failure site passes a constant. leaf's diagnostic PRODUCTION already satisfies "a diagnostic is a value, never an effect" in full; the entire PT-01 problem is delivery-side (utils.ts:33's gate, parser.ts:67-68's coupled `console.error`) and needs no change in this module.

missed.claim: `regex(r, matchFunction)` can advance the parse offset NEGATIVELY, rewinding to 0 mid-parse and defeating the zero-advance guard that L·S-1/S-2 praise — an unbounded `many()` loop reachable from the published leaf

Per ES semantics a sticky/global `exec` that fails sets `lastIndex = 0`, and the published signature at leaf.ts:319 is `(match: RegExpMatchArray | null) => string | null` — a NULL argument with a non-null return is the declared contract, not an abuse. `state.ok(value, offset)` does `this.offset += offset` (state.ts:55-57), so the advance is `0 - savedOffset` and the offset jumps BACKWARD to 0. The only liveness guards in the library are `if (state.offset === savedOffset) break;` (parser.ts:538, many) and `if (state.isError || state.offset === savedOffset)` (parser.ts:605, sepBy) — both `===`, both blind to a negative advance. So `regex(r, fn).many()` where fn synthesises a default on no-match re-parses from offset 0 forever, pushing an element each pass: hang plus unbounded array growth. This directly falsifies L·S-2's unqualified "neither can hang many() or sepBy()" and L·S-1's framing of the library as fail-loud at numeric boundaries. Neither challenge reads the matchFunction branch at all — L·B-2 cites leaf.ts:342 only for the drop-undefined arm two lines below.

NEW (mine) — `sepBy`'s trailing-separator rejection is genuinely correct, and rarer than the packrat unwind. parser.ts:594-611 checkpoints at `cpBeforeSep` BEFORE the separator, and when the element after a separator fails OR matches ε it restores to `cpBeforeSep` rather than to the post-separator offset (:605-610) — so `"a,b,"` yields ["a","b"] with the offset parked on the comma for the caller to reject, and a zero-width element cannot grow the list. Most combinator libraries either accept the trailing separator or backtrack to the wrong checkpoint. The doc comment at parser.ts:565-568 states the contract ("Never accepts a trailing separator — trailing sep acceptance is a grammar concern") and the code keeps it. Neither challenge records it.

Since regex terminals are the dominant leaf of every grammar in the band (parser-band.md:108), this is the single highest-leverage allocation decision in the package, and it is correct. L·M-1 counts the second sticky RegExp compiled per `regex()` call (leaf.ts:322) as a cost without noting it is the price of this win.
